analysis.one_liner: Requires large companies to audit and report the automated systems they use in hiring, lending, housing, and health decisions.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 11 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require large companies to study and document the effects of the automated decision systems they use in high-stakes areas — hiring, credit, housing, health care, education, and utilities — and to report a summary to the Federal Trade Commission, which would publish findings in a public repository. Companies would also have to try to fix systems found to cause material harm, including harm that falls differently by race, sex, age, or disability. Enforcement would run through the FTC and state attorneys general, and state consumer laws would remain intact.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers whose lives are shaped by algorithmic decisions — job applicants screened by software, renters and borrowers scored by models, patients routed by systems — would gain notice, contest and appeal mechanisms, and a public FTC repository documenting who is using which automated systems to make which decisions. Advocates and researchers would gain data to study the systems.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers facing algorithmic decisions in jobs, credit, housing

how_it_helps.text: Companies above the bill's size thresholds would have to perform ongoing impact assessments of automated decision systems used in 'critical decisions' — employment, financial services, housing, health care, education, utilities, and family planning — before and after deployment.

Impact assessments would have to evaluate differential performance by race, sex, age, disability, and other characteristics, and companies would have to attempt to eliminate or mitigate any likely material negative impact.

Companies would have to document and assess mechanisms for consumers to contest, correct, or appeal an automated decision or opt out, and the FTC would publish a searchable public repository of summary reports.
The FTC would gain a new Bureau of Technology with at least 50 technologist staff plus 25 additional enforcement staff, and state attorneys general could sue violators on behalf of residents.

analysis.who_pays: Large technology companies, data-driven lenders, employers, landlords, and other firms above the bill's thresholds would bear the cost of ongoing audits, documentation, consultation with outside stakeholders, and annual FTC reporting. Firms under the thresholds (roughly $50 million in receipts or $5 million for sellers of decision systems) are exempt.

drawbacks.text: The full impact assessments would not be public: companies must share only a limited summary report with the FTC, and the bill expressly says nothing requires disclosure of the underlying assessment to the Commission or the public beyond that summary.

Compliance is an added cost on large firms, and the bill leaves it to FTC rulemaking to define, prioritize, and phase in the requirements, with regulations taking effect two years after they are promulgated — so real-world benefits would arrive slowly and depend heavily on how the FTC writes the rules.
Smaller companies that still make consequential algorithmic decisions fall below the covered-entity thresholds and would face no requirements.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's approach is accountability-by-paperwork rather than prohibition: it does not ban any automated practice, but forces the largest users of algorithmic decision-making to test for bias, document harms, and report to a regulator that would publish findings publicly. The main weaknesses are that the underlying assessments stay confidential, small firms are exempt, and enforcement depends entirely on FTC rules that would take years to write. Still, for consumers on the receiving end of opaque systems in hiring, credit, housing, and health care, it would create the first broad paper trail — and the compliance cost falls on precisely the large firms whose systems the bill covers.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee for the rest of the two-year Congress and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Senator Ron Wyden introduced the Algorithmic Accountability Act of 2023 on September 21, 2023, with 11 Democratic cosponsors: Booker, Heinrich, Peters, Casey, Lujan, Baldwin, Merkley, Whitehouse, Schatz, Hirono, and Warren.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
That referral was the last action of any kind on the bill; the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with the bill still in committee, with no reported version, no hearing, and no vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that use automated decision systems in hiring, lending, housing, and health care — including large tech platforms and the vendors that sell those systems — are better off, because they avoided new audit, documentation, and reporting requirements. Consumers gained nothing, since the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies that avoided algorithmic accountability rules

for.name: Ron Wyden
for.role: U.S. Senator from Oregon; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on September 21, 2023 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no report — for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never advanced in a Senate where Democrats held a narrow majority.

industries.industry: Large technology platforms and AI system developers
industries.note: The bill would make the biggest users and sellers of automated decision systems document, test for bias, and report on systems used in hiring, credit, housing, and health care. Its failure leaves those systems unregulated at the federal level, and the industry's interest in avoiding the audits ran against consumers' interest in accountability.

Firms above the bill's thresholds that rely on algorithmic screening in finance, employment, and housing would have faced ongoing impact assessments, bias testing by race, sex, age, and disability, and annual FTC reporting. The bill's death preserves the status quo, in which consumers rarely know an algorithm made the decision.

The bill would have pushed companies toward third-party audits, privacy-enhancing technologies, and stakeholder consultation, creating demand for auditing and privacy-engineering services. Its failure means that market does not materialize.
